claims.text: Adding roughly 2–5 at.% Si to the boride-based alloy will improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
Si addition will promote in situ formation of a continuous Si-rich intermetallic barrier at the alloy surface during service.
Current boride-based components have a standard undoped boride microstructure and phase distribution.
The Si-doped alloy can be produced through the same melting and casting route as the undoped baseline.
A 2–5 at.% Si range is suitable for producing the proposed corrosion-resistant alloy.
Typical hot-dip aluminum-plating exposure occurs at approximately 660 °C.
The intervention should remain effective when Si is maintained at 2–5 at.% and temperatures remain near standard operating conditions.
Exposure to molten aluminum will form a thin, continuous Si-rich intermetallic or silicide layer on the alloy surface.
The Si-rich surface layer will act as a diffusion barrier and limit interfacial attack.
Si segregates during high-temperature exposure and reacts with the boride matrix to form a stable, adherent Si-rich layer.
The Si-rich layer decreases the wettability of the alloy by molten aluminum.
The Si-rich layer retards dissolution or penetration of the underlying boride phases and thereby reduces corrosion kinetics.
At plating temperatures, the Si-doped alloy will show approximately 30–50% less penetration depth or weight loss than the undoped alloy over the same exposure time.
Undoped boride-based components experience measurable molten-aluminum corrosion under hot-dip plating conditions.
Si contents below the proposed range may be insufficient to form a continuous protective layer.
Large deviations from normal operating temperature may degrade the protective barrier.
